1.descripcion: Founded by Alfonso II 'El Casto' as part of the episcopal complex in Oviedo. Although it has undergone numerous alterations over the centuries (the current façade is Baroque), it retains from its pre-Romanesque origins the end wall of the chancel with its distinctive three-light window featuring semicircular arches and columns with Visigothic capitals. This tripartite window has become one of the visual icons of Asturian art.

2.descripcion: A two-storey palatine chapel incorporated into Oviedo Cathedral. The upper level (San Miguel) houses the relics of the Holy Ark and the Crosses of Victory and the Angels, symbols of Asturias. The lower level (Saint Leocadia) features a barrel vault. Of particular note is the Romanesque apostles’ group added later to its columns, which is one of the most important sculptural ensembles of the 12th century in Spain. It originally formed part of Alfonso II's palatine complex.

3.descripcion: Commonly known as Santullano, it is the largest and oldest church from the Asturian period. Commissioned by Alfonso II, it is notable for its vast size, its basilica-style layout with a raised transept and, above all, for its exceptional cycle of aniconic wall paintings featuring geometric and architectural motifs that originally covered all its interior walls. This pictorial programme, unique in Western Europe at the time, demonstrates continuity with the late Roman pictorial tradition.

4.descripcion: A basilical structure following the model of Santullano, albeit on a smaller scale. It was rebuilt after suffering severe damage in 1936 during the Spanish Civil War. Its large narthex or entrance portico and the layout of its side aisles are particularly noteworthy, making it a key example of the style during the reign of Alfonso II. Its hilltop location overlooks the valley, highlighting the strategic and symbolic importance of such buildings.

5.descripcion: A basilical church with three naves separated by semicircular arches resting on square pillars, situated in a rural setting beside the River Nora. It features a tripartite chancel characteristic of Asturian art. Despite its almost complete reconstruction following the Civil War (led by the architect Luis Menéndez Pidal), it retains the purity of line and the architectural restraint characteristic of Asturian art.

6.descripcion: A masterpiece of the Ramirense period. Originally designed as a royal hall or pleasure palace on the outskirts of Oviedo, it was converted into a church in the 12th century. It is notable for its innovative architecture: a two-storey rectangular structure with side galleries (belvederes) featuring blind arcades, a barrel vault reinforced with interior transverse arches, and exquisite sculptural decoration on medallions and capitals. It represents the pinnacle of pre-Romanesque European architecture.

7.descripcion: A palatine church dedicated to Saint Michael the Archangel, situated just a few metres from the Naranco and forming part of this royal complex. Currently, only the western third of the original structure remains, following a collapse in the 13th century. It is famous for the slenderness of its proportions, its carved stone tracery featuring geometric motifs (some of which are unique in European art) and the reliefs on its jambs, inspired by a Roman consular diptych, bearing witness to an interest in the classical past.

8.descripcion: A small gem from the Ramirense period, situated on a hill with panoramic views of the Caudal Valley. Its most distinctive feature is the iconostasis: a triple stone archway separating the chancel from the nave, decorated with reused Visigothic elements. This structure, together with the side galleries, creates a hierarchically organised space designed for liturgical use. Its Greek cross plan and the quality of its ashlar masonry demonstrate the maturity of the Ramirense style.

9.descripcion: The only surviving example of a pre-Romanesque Asturian public utility building still standing in its original location. It consists of a drinking fountain sheltered by a stone pavilion with a semicircular arch. The Cross of Victory is displayed on the pediment, together with its inscription. Although traditionally attributed to the reign of Alfonso III, recent studies suggest that it may have been built during the reign of Alfonso II, without completely ruling out the possibility of a Roman origin. It is an exceptional example of early medieval hydraulic engineering.

10.descripcion: This church, with its simple structure and three-nave basilica-style layout, was commissioned by Alfonso III and his wife Jimena as part of a monastery. It preserves significant remains of the original wall paintings in the chancel, featuring geometric and plant motifs. It stands as a key testament to the expansion of the Asturian kingdom into the inland valleys of the Cantabrian Mountains and to royal patronage in the repopulation of these territories.

11.descripcion: Popularly known as 'El Conventín', it represents the apogee of the Alfonsine period. Set in the lush natural surroundings of the Boides Valley, it forms part of a larger monastery. It is notable for its open side portico (unique in Asturian pre-Romanesque architecture) and for maintaining a perfect balance between traditional Asturian influences and the new Mozarabic elements introduced by craftsmen from Al-Andalus, heralding the Romanesque style.

12.descripcion: Consecrated in the 10th century, it closely follows the architectural design of Santullano, albeit from a later period. It retains a significant portion of its original pictorial decoration on the interior walls and triumphal arches, with Mozarabic influences. It serves as a transitional link between the pure Asturian style and the early Romanesque style that was beginning to take shape in the rest of Europe, maintaining local tradition whilst incorporating innovations from the new style to come.

13.descripcion: Located near the eastern coast of Asturias (Colunga), this imposing church is notable for the elegance of its proportions and the quality of its rough-hewn stonework. It underwent extensive renovation in the 18th century (with the addition of a Baroque bell gable), but modern restoration work has restored its pre-Romanesque character, which is particularly evident in the tripartite chancel and the capitals decorated with plant and geometric motifs.
